operations.evidence: STATS19 covers personal-injury road collisions on public roads that become known to the police within 30 days.
It does not cover every collision or every road-safety event.
Damage-only collisions with no human casualty are outside the reported road casualty statistics.
Property-damage incidents must not be counted as injury collisions.
Collisions on private roads or in car parks are outside the core STATS19 scope.
Absence from STATS19 does not imply absence of a private-site collision.
Around 50 data items are collected for each in-scope collision, including time, location, vehicles, drivers and casualties.
The existence of detailed fields does not guarantee that each record is complete or correct.
Police or their agents process STATS19 records and provide them for Department for Transport checking and analysis.
Administrative processing introduces possible recording and transfer errors.
STATS19 is not a complete record of all injury collisions and casualties.
Counts must not be treated as the true total number of road injuries.
When drivers exchange details, there may be no legal obligation to report an injury collision to police, contributing to under-reporting.
Unreported collisions cannot be assigned to parcels from STATS19 data.
Under-reporting includes collisions not reported to police and collisions reported but not recorded.
Missing records do not support a zero-risk conclusion.
Only a small proportion of some single-vehicle pedal-cycle injury collisions are reported to police.
Police data can disproportionately understate some road-user groups.
It can be difficult for police officers to classify casualties as slight or serious at the roadside.
Raw severity labels may contain judgment error.
Injury-based reporting systems are associated with increased numbers classified as serious injuries.
Trend breaks can reflect recording-system change rather than real severity change.
STATS19 errors can arise from uncompleted forms, misreported details and processing failures by police or local authorities.
Validation reduces but does not eliminate administrative error.
Police, local authorities and the Department for Transport use multiple validation layers.
A validated dataset still retains some missing and incorrect information.
Validation checks that collision grid references fall within the relevant local-authority boundary.
Boundary validation does not prove survey-grade positional accuracy or parcel identity.
Department for Transport validation checks for duplicate collision records.
Duplicate checking does not guarantee every duplicate is detected.
Validation checks for orphan casualty or vehicle records without an associated collision.
Relational consistency does not establish factual accuracy of the underlying event.
Validation errors are classified as hard, severe or other, and unresolved lower-priority inconsistent values may be set to unknown.
Unknown values must not be imputed as specific local attributes without a documented method.
Most validation occurs after a full year of data and the database is closed for annual statistical production after corrections.
Earlier extracts may differ from final annual data.
Provisional road casualty figures use less validation and may estimate missing data before final annual figures are available.
Provisional estimates must not be presented as final exact counts.
Reported road casualty statistics are useful for broad trend analysis but do not provide a complete parcel-level safety score.
A local or parcel risk result requires separate spatial, temporal and completeness evidence.
